Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine.
The NHS says it works by killing the fungus, or yeast, that is causing the infection.
It makes holes in the fungus's cell membrane so that the contents leak out.
Azole antifungals are described as blocking a step in the making of ergosterol, the main fat-like building block of fungal cell membranes.
For vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush the NHS says symptoms should be better within a week; serious fungal infections take longer.
Stomach pain or discomfort, diarrhoea, headache, feeling or being sick and rash are listed, with nausea and diarrhoea the most frequent.
Some people feel dizzy; the NHS advises waiting until it passes before driving or using machinery.
Severe vomiting or diarrhoea can reduce the protection of the contraceptive pill.
A severe allergic reaction or a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome needs a 999 call.
Liver problems can show as yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or pale stools; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 for serious side effects other than emergencies.
Easy bruising or infections, which may point to a blood disorder, and a faster or irregular heartbeat are also listed as warning signs.
note: NHS via summary; route is NHS 111 per summary
